LLM MRI, 23 Nov 2026. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, EXL3 3.05 bpw, one 7900 XTX.

An MRI of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: what lights up while it writes

Each answer from this model passes through 48 layers of 512 small experts, and a router picks 10 of them per layer for every token. I logged those picks while it answered 512 prompts on 64 topics (PHP, Polish, legal text, cooking, emoji posts and so on), like a brain scan taken during different tasks. Then I named every expert by the topic that lights it up.

The short version:

  • 9,903 of the 24,576 routed experts (48 layers × 512, top 10 per token) have one clear topic.
  • The sharpest one is L47.E174. It fires 948× more on Dutch than on anything else.
  • Layers 8–23 and 24–39 are twins. Expert E at layer L usually does the same job as expert E at L+16.
  • No topic gets its own private path. Most PHP traffic goes through experts shared by all code.

What I found

  
Specialists are real. 40% of experts have a clear specialty. Dutch (L47.E174, 948×), translation (L17.E287, 710×), Hindi (L36.E111, 528×) and legal text (L44.E453, 516×) each have experts that almost never fire for anything else.

  
Twin layers. Expert E in layer L (8–23) has the same specialty as expert E in L+16 in 67–83% of cases. At any other offset the match rate is about 1.5%. Their router rows have cosine 0.84–0.93; shuffled pairs score about 0.3. The likely cause is depth up-scaling: layers 24–39 were initialised as a copy of 8–23 and then trained further.

  
Language experts sit late. Human-language specialists (Polish, Korean, Dutch…) are concentrated in layers 36–47, where the next word is chosen. Subject experts such as finance, physics and chemistry cluster at L15/L31. Layers 0–7 are the least specialised (32% of experts have a topic, against 49% in layers 40–47).

  
No topic owns its routing. On average only about 29% of a topic's traffic goes to its own specialists or its family's shared experts (e.g. “code (general)”). About 35% goes to experts labelled for other topics, 6% to generalists and 30% to “rare” experts that fire too little to label. PHP is the most self-contained topic at about 45%, but only 3% is pure-PHP experts and 42% is shared code experts.


  
How the router works

  
    
    
  • Every token, at every one of the 48 MoE layers, takes its 2560-dim hidden state and multiplies it by the router matrix mlp.gate.weight (512 × 2560). That gives 512 scores.
    • 
    
  • The top 10 scores win. Their softmax weights are renormalised to sum to 1, and those 10 experts' outputs are mixed with those weights. A shared expert (gated by a sigmoid) always runs as well.
    • 
    
  • Each expert is a small SwiGLU MLP: gate, up and down projections of 2560 × 640, so 640 “neurons” and 4.9 M weights. That is about 1.9 MB at 3 bits per weight.
    • 
    
  • Nothing tells the router about topics. Specialisation emerges in training, nudged by a small load-balancing loss (coef 0.001) that keeps any one expert from hogging traffic.
    • 
  


  
How the names were made

  
    
    
  • I added a small patch to the inference server that logs, per request, how often each expert is picked during generation. The extra MTP (draft) layer is left out.
    • 
    
  • I sent 512 prompts: 8 per topic across 64 topics in 5 families (code, data formats, human languages, subjects, writing styles).
    • 
    
  • For each expert and topic I computed the share of routes and the lift versus all other topics and versus sibling topics (e.g. PHP vs other code). An expert is a domain specialist if min(lift) ≥ 5 and it fired in ≥ 75% of that topic's prompts. It is a family expert if it covers a whole family (lift ≥ 4), a generalist if it fires everywhere, and rare otherwise.
    • 
    
  • Result: 9,903 domain, 3,492 family, 498 generalist and 10,683 rare experts.
    • 
  


  
The PHP case

  
PHP has 25 clean specialists, about 120 M weights (46 MB at 3 bpw). The top few fire on more than 80% of PHP tokens: L43.E291, L46.E000, L42.E408, the twins L18.E135 and L34.E135, L40.E237, and L44.E388. In principle you could fine-tune just these experts to improve PHP without touching C. In practice, more than half of PHP's traffic goes to shared code experts, so a change there leaks into other languages.


  
Caveats

  
    
    
  • Only decode tokens are counted, aggregated per request, not per token. A “PHP expert” could be the “closing brace after a PHP string” expert.
    • 
    
  • 8 prompts per topic. Labels give the best match, not exclusive ownership. Low-traffic experts are noisy.
    • 
    
  • The model is quantised (EXL3 3.05 bpw). Routing on full-precision weights may differ slightly.
    •
